title: Week 4: Presentation of Action Plans
text:
Week 4 Live · approx. 2h (async option available) Presentations & discussion



The closing session brings the course’s individual work together: participants present their completed ESD Action Plans, identify opportunities for collaboration, and reflect on and evaluate the course as a whole.

title: Week 4: Presentation of Action Plans
text:
Session Overview







Format
Recommended as a live synchronous session (on-site or video call), since it centers on presentations and live group discussion. If a live session is not feasible: run as a time-boxed asynchronous window (e.g. one week) with recorded action-plan presentations and written peer feedback in place of live presentation and discussion.


Duration
Approx. 2h live (scales with group size, given 6-minute presentations per participant/group). Asynchronous equivalent: an open review window of several days, with roughly 60-90 minutes of individual engagement time (viewing others’ presentations, giving feedback, completing the evaluation).


Preparation for participants
A completed ESD Action Plan (Tasks after Sessions 1-3), and a prepared short presentation of it (approx. 6 minutes)

title: Week 4: Presentation of Action Plans
text:
Learning Objectives
By the end of this session, participants will be able to:

Deepen their understanding of ESD and constructive alignment.
Present their own action plan.
Identify collaboration opportunities with other lecturers, departments, or external organizations working on sustainability initiatives.

title: Week 4: Presentation of Action Plans
text:
Session Outline


1. Muddiest point (variable, approx. 10 min)

Addressing points of confusion raised after Session 3.

2. Presentation of Action Plans (variable, 6 min per participant)

Current state, opportunities identified, developed session (learning outcomes, activities, assessment); listeners take notes and prepare feedback.

3. Synthesis (10 min)

Key insights across the presented action plans (challenges, need for further support, etc.).


4. Group discussion: collaboration opportunities (10 min)

5. Harvesting of the group discussion (10 min)

Highlights, synergies, commonalities.


6. Open Q&A (10 min)
7. Main learnings from the course and course evaluation (variable, approx. 10 min)

title: Week 4: Presentation of Action Plans
text:
Preparation tasks & learning activities






Before the session
Finalize the ESD Action Plan (Tasks after Sessions 1-3) and prepare a short (approx. 6-minute) presentation of it.









During the session

Present (or submit a recorded presentation of) your action plan.
Take notes and prepare constructive feedback on other participants’ presentations.
Contribute to the group discussion on collaboration opportunities.
Complete the course evaluation survey.










After the session
No formal task is defined in the course materials after this closing session. Consider suggesting, as an optional next step, that participants share their action plan with their department or apply it in an upcoming course.

title: Week 4: Presentation of Action Plans
text:
Recommendation for facilitation

Use a shared virtual board (e.g. Miro) for noting down the collaboration-opportunities discussion, and a live polling tool (e.g. Menti) for the “main learnings” question.
In a live session, the “main learnings of the course” question works well as an open plenary discussion following the live poll, giving participants a chance to hear and build on each other’s takeaways, not just see them aggregated. In a self-paced/asynchronous format, replace this with an individual written reflection using the same prompt.
Since action plans span many disciplines, structure peer feedback prompts to ask specifically how a presented idea could translate to a different field, not just whether it works well within its own discipline; this is where the cross-disciplinary value of the session lies.
Where a fully live session with all participants is not feasible, keep the peer-feedback element by running a time-boxed asynchronous window with recorded presentations and written comments, rather than dropping it.
Closing evaluation: the course should close with an evaluation, adapted to reflect the actual format in which it was delivered, the content covered, the delivery mode (live vs. self-paced vs. hybrid), and, where relevant, the specific adaptations made for that cohort’s context.

title: Week 3: Education for Sustainable Development (ESD) & Constructive Alignment
text:
Week 3 Self-paced online · 95-105 min Plenary



This session turns from concepts to course design. It introduces Education for Sustainable Development as a distinct pedagogical approach, and constructive alignment as the design tool that translates ESD principles into a concrete, well-aligned course unit or course.

title: Week 3: Education for Sustainable Development (ESD) & Constructive Alignment
text:
Recommendation for facilitation

Use a shared digital board (e.g. Padlet) or an equivalent tool for the “muddiest point” task, so responses can be reviewed and addressed collectively. As facilitator, review all “muddiest points” before the next session and prepare answers for the questions raised.
After presenting the land degradation and urban migration examples, ask participants to sketch how the same three-element alignment could look for a topic in their own discipline, this is where transfer actually happens.
The “teaching principles” reflection works well as a cross-disciplinary sharing moment: participants from different fields often name different principles.

title: Week 1: Introduction to Sustainable Development
text:
Recommendation for facilitation

Use an interactive polling tool (e.g. Mentimeter) for the “Earth from space” word-cloud opening in a live session.
Keep the SDG relevance exercise open-ended rather than pre-selecting example goals, so participants from different disciplines can each anchor it to their own field.
Given how much content the theories section covers, split it into two shorter learning units (historical milestones 1970-2000; contemporary frameworks 2009-2023) rather than one long block.
For the Ethiopia/Kenya pilot cohorts, pairing the UN SDGs with the AU Agenda 2063 resonated well as a regionally grounded complement to the global framework. When adapting this course for participants elsewhere, look for a comparable regional or national framework to pair with the SDGs, since Agenda 2063 will not be equally relevant to all users of this course.

title: CDE - Open Education Resources
text:
About this course
This course was developed in 2023 by a tri-national (Swiss, Kenyan, and Ethiopian) project team of nine members, representing:

University of Bern, Switzerland (Centre for Development and Environment)
Addis Ababa University, Ethiopia (Water and Land Resource Centre, and College of Education and Behavioral Studies)
University of Nairobi, Kenya (Department of Geography, Population and Environmental Studies, and the Centre for Training and Integrated Research on ASAL Development)

The team iteratively built and revised the course’s four sessions through collaborative working groups. The course was first piloted online with higher education faculty in Kenya in 2024, and on-site in Ethiopia in 2025. Following revision based on both pilots, it is now available for wider adoption.

Course objective
The course is designed to empower higher education lecturers in Ethiopia and Kenya with the knowledge, tools, and strategies to effectively integrate sustainable development (SD) and SD concepts and theories into their teaching. It provides an in-depth understanding of key SD concepts and theories, guides participants in establishing thematic connections between sustainable development and their own field, and highlights the importance of Education for Sustainable Development (ESD) for sustainable futures.


Target group
The course is aimed at higher education teaching staff from all disciplines. Decision-makers and academic programme directors may also find it valuable to attend.


How you can use this course
There are several ways to engage with this material, depending on your needs:

Work through the course independently, at your own pace: All four sessions, materials, and exercises are freely available for self-paced learning — use them as they are, or draw on individual sections and materials for your own purposes.
Adapt and deliver the course at your own institution: The sessions, examples, and exercises can be localized to your own context — the illustrative cases used throughout (from Switzerland, Ethiopia, and Kenya) are meant as models, not fixed content, and are designed to be substituted with examples relevant to your own setting.
Co-design a course with us: If you are interested in developing a tailored version of this course together with the original project team, we welcome the opportunity to collaborate — please get in touch to discuss what this could look like [contact details to be confirmed].

title: Adapt & Reuse
text:
Adapting This Course

This course is designed to be adopted and adapted by Higher Education Institutions worldwide. Everything here — sessions, slides, frameworks, assessment designs — is published under CC BY 4.0. You are free to take what you need, leave what you don’t, and build something better. This page explains how.




1. Use individual sessions
You do not need to run the whole course. Any session can stand alone as a guest lecture, workshop module, or seminar input. Each session page is self-contained with learning objectives, materials, tasks, and a localisation note.
How: Download the session QMD file from GitHub, or copy the content into your own course design.


2. Swap in local case studies
Every session includes a localisation note — a yellow panel at the bottom of the page — that guides you on how to replace our default examples (often European or generic global) with cases from your own regional context.
How: Follow the localisation note. If you develop a strong local example, please share it via a GitHub pull request so other institutions can benefit.


3. Translate
All materials are licensed for translation. A German version is in preparation at CDE. If you translate materials into another language, please notify the course team so we can link to your version from the repository.
How: Fork the GitHub repository, edit the QMD files, and publish your translated version.


4. Remix and extend
Add sessions, change the sequence, integrate your own assessments, or embed this course within a larger programme. The Quarto format makes structural edits straightforward.
How: Fork the repository. The _quarto.yml navigation and sessions/index.qmd listing control the structure. _variables.yml lets you update course metadata in one place.


5. Run a co-taught version
This course was designed for co-teaching across institutions. The case presentations (Weeks 9–10) and the field session (Week 11) are especially powerful when run jointly between partner institutions via video link.
How: Contact the CDE coordination team at cde@unibe.ch to discuss scheduling a joint cohort with another partner institution.


6. Contribute back
The course improves when institutions share what they changed and why. Contributions welcome: new case studies, updated readings, improved localisation notes, translations, additional sessions.
How: Open an issue or pull request on the GitHub repository. All contributors are acknowledged in the course team page.

title: Adapt & Reuse
text:
Technical Setup
The course is built with Quarto — an open-source scientific publishing system. You need Quarto installed to render the site locally.
Quick start:
# 1. Clone the repository
git clone https://github.com/CDEteaching/[REPO-NAME].git
cd [REPO-NAME]

# 2. Install Quarto (see https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/)

# 3. Preview locally
quarto preview

# 4. Render to _site/ folder
quarto render
Deployment to GitHub Pages is automated via the included GitHub Actions workflow (.github/workflows/publish.yml). Push to main and the site rebuilds automatically.
Editing in RStudio: Open the project folder in RStudio — it will detect the Quarto project automatically. Use the Render button to preview individual pages.

Reflection Journal Guidelines
The reflection journal is a weekly 300–400 word entry responding to a prompt from each session. Entries are submitted via the course platform within one week of each session.
Grading: Journals are graded holistically at the end of the course on depth of engagement (40%), use of course concepts (40%), and intellectual honesty — including expressing genuine uncertainty (20%). There is no penalty for “wrong” answers; the journal rewards careful thinking.

title: Week 1 Reader: Introduction to Sustainable Development
text:
Why “sustainable development”? Framing the session
The session opens with the 1968 “Earthrise” photograph, taken during the Apollo 8 mission, the first time humans saw the whole Earth from space. The image is used deliberately, not as decoration: it is widely credited with shifting public perception of the planet from an unlimited backdrop for human activity to something small, bounded, and shared. That shift, from an implicitly limitless world to a finite one, is the intuitive starting point for everything that follows in this course.

title: Week 1 Reader: Introduction to Sustainable Development
text:
Defining Sustainable Development
The most widely used definition of sustainable development comes from the 1987 report Our Common Future, produced by the World Commission on Environment and Development (WCED) under the Norwegian Prime Minister Gro Harlem Brundtland, and known ever since as the Brundtland Report:

“Development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.”

This definition was adopted by the United Nations Conference on Environment and Development (Rio, 1992) and has since become the default global reference point, including in Switzerland’s own understanding of sustainable development. Two things are worth noticing about it: it introduces an explicit temporal dimension (present versus future generations), and it says nothing about how needs should be met, which is exactly why the concept has been filled with very different content ever since.
Alongside the temporal dimension, sustainable development is conventionally broken down into three substantive dimensions: environment (resource management, pollution, biodiversity), society (quality of life, education, equity), and economy (employment, productivity, cost of living). This three-dimension model, used for example in Switzerland’s MONET sustainability monitoring system, is easy to communicate and therefore widespread, but it can also obscure aspects that do not map neatly onto any one of the three, such as culture, technology, or health, which is why some models extend it to four dimensions or represent the dimensions as nested (economy within society within environment) rather than as three equal, separate circles.
This conceptual looseness is also the concept’s main weakness: sustainable development has been criticised as conceptually fuzzy, as having no clear priority ranking between its dimensions, as blurring the line between methods and goals, and as a concept “everyone can agree to” precisely because it lacks specificity. One influential way of sharpening the concept is the distinction between weak and strong sustainability, which asks whether natural capital can be substituted by human-made capital (weak) or must be protected as a non-negotiable minimum (strong).
📖 Textbook: Brundtland Commission · Three dimensions of sustainability · A four-dimensional model of sustainability · Weak and strong sustainability

title: Week 1 Reader: Introduction to Sustainable Development
section: Agenda 2063 and the Sustainable Development Goals
text:
Agenda 2063 and the Sustainable Development Goals
In 2015, all 193 UN member states adopted the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, with its 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and 169 targets, covering everything from poverty and hunger to climate action and institutional justice. The SDGs succeeded the earlier Millennium Development Goals (2000-2015), which had been criticised for being defined mainly by industrialised countries, lacking binding commitments, and relying on unrealistic targets.
The African Union’s Agenda 2063, “The Africa We Want,” is a parallel, continent-specific framework built around seven aspirations: a prosperous and integrated Africa, good governance, peace and security, a strong cultural identity, people-driven development, and a strong global role. Rather than treating Agenda 2063 as a regional footnote to the SDGs, the session presents them side by side and asks participants to work out the overlaps and gaps themselves, since the two frameworks share substantial common ground but were negotiated through different political processes.






Note



Adapting this for your own region
Agenda 2063 pairs naturally with the SDGs for African cohorts, but it is a regional framework, not a universal complement. If you are teaching this course elsewhere, look for a comparable regional or national development framework (an ASEAN framework, an EU strategy, a national development plan) to pair with the SDGs instead, so participants can anchor the global framework in the political context they actually work in.


📖 Textbook: The 2030 Agenda and the SDGs · Agenda 21: Think globally, act locally

title: Week 1 Reader: Introduction to Sustainable Development
text:
Sustainability challenges: why the urgency
Since 1950, almost every indicator of human activity, population, GDP, energy use, water use, fertiliser consumption, and every indicator of Earth-system change, greenhouse gas concentration, ocean acidification, biodiversity loss, has grown in a pattern that Steffen et al. (2015) call the “Great Acceleration.” The point of the graph is not any single number but the shape: near-flat for most of human history, then a sharp bend upward exactly at the mid-20th century.
Two further data sources are used to make the scale of the challenge concrete. The World Economic Forum’s annual Global Risks Report, based on a survey of over a thousand experts, has for several years ranked environmental risks (extreme weather, failure to mitigate climate change, biodiversity loss) among the most severe global risks over both short and long time horizons. And Fanning et al. (2022) combine planetary-boundary and social-threshold data for individual countries into a single chart: it shows that essentially no country yet manages to provide a social foundation for its population without overshooting at least one planetary boundary, which is precisely the “safe and just space” the Doughnut model (see below) is trying to define.
📖 Textbook: Debates about planetary boundaries · From planetary boundaries to the doughnut model

title: Week 1 Reader: Introduction to Sustainable Development
section: Sustainability theories and UN conferences: a short history
text:
Sustainability theories and UN conferences: a short history
The session traces a timeline from 1970 to the present, alternating between theoretical milestones and international political milestones:








Year
Theory / concept
International milestone




1972
Limits to Growth (Club of Rome / MIT computer models)
UN Conference on the Human Environment, Stockholm


1987
Three-circles model of sustainability emerges
Brundtland Report, Our Common Future


1992

Earth Summit, Rio de Janeiro (UNCED)


2000

Millennium Development Goals


2009
Planetary Boundaries (Rockström et al.)



2012
Doughnut Model (Raworth)
Rio+20


2013

Agenda 2063 (African Union)


2015

2030 Agenda / SDGs



A few of these are worth unpacking further. The Limits to Growth (1972), produced by a group of scientists associated with the Club of Rome, used some of the first computer models of global resource use to run scenarios of population, industrial output, food production, pollution, and resource depletion. Its “standard run,” assuming no change in historical patterns, showed industrial growth slowing sharply once resource depletion outpaces the ability to extract new resources, followed eventually by falling population. The book is often credited with an early use of the word “sustainable” and remains contested: critics point out it does not account well for technological change or the changing definition of what counts as a usable resource, but it was influential precisely because it was among the first attempts to model the finiteness of the Earth system formally, prefiguring today’s planetary boundaries work.
The 1992 Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro brought together 179 countries and produced five major documents: the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), the Convention on Biological Diversity, the Rio Declaration on Environment and Development, Agenda 21, and a Statement of Principles on Forests, plus groundwork for what became the UN Convention to Combat Desertification. Twenty years later, Rio+20 (2012) was widely judged a comparatively modest outcome document, but it launched the process that led directly to the SDGs, and it formalised early guidelines on green economy policy.
📖 Textbook: Club of Rome and The Limits to Growth · From Rio 1992 to today · Rio+20 · The debate about the Great Transformation

title: Week 1 Reader: Introduction to Sustainable Development
section: Whose sustainability? Worldviews and the many values of nature
text:
Whose sustainability? Worldviews and the many values of nature
Pascual et al. (2023), drawing on work for the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services (IPBES), argue that different worldviews shape how people relate to nature in ways that go beyond a simple pro-environment/anti-environment axis. They distinguish, broadly: living from and living in nature (anthropocentric framings, prioritising human interests), living with nature (bio- or ecocentric framings, treating other living beings or ecological processes as having value in their own right), and living as nature (pluralistic framings, emphasising the interdependence of humans, other beings, and systemic processes). The point for this course is practical, not just philosophical: a sustainability initiative designed on one of these framings (say, valuing a forest purely for its carbon-storage or tourism revenue) can look entirely different, and generate different conflicts, from one designed on another (valuing the same forest as a living system with its own integrity, or as inseparable from a community’s identity).

title: Week 1 Reader: Introduction to Sustainable Development
text:
Key messages

The three (or more) dimensions of sustainable development are interlinked at every level, not separable in practice.
Sustainable development is a complex, internationally negotiated concept, not a fixed technical standard.
The challenges it responds to are accelerating, and the case for urgency is not rhetorical, it shows up directly in the data.
Context matters: what “sustainable development” should mean and prioritise depends on where you are, and whose values and worldview are doing the defining.

title: Week 1 Reader: Introduction to Sustainable Development
section: Looking ahead: the ESD Action Plan
text:
Looking ahead: the ESD Action Plan
Session 1 also opens the course’s overarching assignment: building an ESD Action Plan across the four sessions. After Session 1, the task is to review how sustainable development is currently reflected in your own teaching; after Session 2, to identify concrete opportunities to bring it in further; after Session 3, to design a full session using constructive alignment; and in Session 4, to present the finished plan and look for collaboration opportunities. The concepts introduced here, the dimensions, the frameworks, the historical grounding, are the vocabulary the rest of the course, and your own Action Plan, will keep returning to.


← Back to Session 01

title: Week 2 Reader: Interlinkages of Sustainability Dimensions and Role of Science & Higher Education
text: This reader expands on the Week 2 slides: it walks through the same concepts in more depth, with the reasoning and sources behind each slide spelled out. Use it to prepare, to revisit after the session, or as a stand-alone text if you are adapting this course and did not attend the live delivery. Also available as a downloadable PDF.

title: Week 2 Reader: Interlinkages of Sustainability Dimensions and Role of Science & Higher Education
text:
From separate dimensions to interlinkages
Week 1 introduced the environmental, social, and economic dimensions of sustainable development largely side by side. Week 2 starts from a simple observation: in practice, no real-world sustainability challenge stays inside one dimension. Different diagrams try to capture this differently. The classic three-circles model treats the dimensions as overlapping but separate; a concentric-circles model instead nests them, economy inside society inside environment, on the argument that society is a subsystem of the environment, and the economy in turn a subsystem of society, so an economy cannot outgrow the social and ecological systems it depends on. The SDGs’ own “wedding cake” model (Stockholm Resilience Centre) makes the same nested argument visually: a biosphere layer at the base, a society layer built on top of it, and an economy layer on top of that, with the 17 SDGs distributed across the three tiers rather than treated as a flat, unordered list.
An Integrated Landscape (Watershed) Management example from Ethiopia (Providoli, 2023) is used to make the interlinkage concrete rather than abstract. Bio-physical measures (rehabilitating the water cycle, improving vegetation cover to reduce erosion, compost and fuel-saving stoves) sit alongside new income-generating activities (home gardens, cash crops, beekeeping) and social-level changes (community grazing management, networking among community groups, extending responsibility to people without formal land rights). None of these measures works in isolation: a purely biophysical intervention without a matching social or economic one tends not to hold, which is exactly the “systemic perspective” the slides emphasise. The same point is made through two further, less resolved cases from Ethiopia: conflict over grazing land and water for cattle, and conflict among people over fishing rights, both cases where environmental scarcity, social relationships, and economic livelihoods are impossible to disentangle.
📖 Textbook: Three dimensions of sustainability · A four-dimensional model of sustainability

title: Week 2 Reader: Interlinkages of Sustainability Dimensions and Role of Science & Higher Education
section: The role of science: from understanding to transformation
text:
The role of science: from understanding to transformation
The session draws directly on the UN’s Global Sustainable Development Report (GSDR) argument that “business as usual is no longer an option” for science and higher education. The claim is specific: science should not stop at understanding human-nature interactions better, it should also actively help change those interactions along more sustainable trajectories. That reframes the research question from “what is happening?” to “how do we orient research so it also helps overcome the problems it describes?”, which in turn requires rethinking how science and society relate to each other and how relevant knowledge gets produced in the first place.
This is usually discussed through three research modes of increasing openness to non-academic input:

Disciplinary research stays within a single discipline.
Interdisciplinary research combines several disciplines.
Transdisciplinary research goes a step further: Jahn, Bergmann & Keil (2012) define it as a reflexive research approach that addresses societal problems through interdisciplinary collaboration and through collaboration between researchers and non-scientific actors (policymakers, practitioners, affected communities), with the explicit aim of enabling mutual learning between science and society, not just extracting data from practitioners. Schneider & Buser (2018), reviewing 16 transdisciplinary projects, found the degree of actual stakeholder interaction varies considerably across the research phases of a project (problem framing, knowledge production, and integration/application), a reminder that “transdisciplinary” is a spectrum, not a label a project either has or lacks.

A table from Herweg (CDE) lines up what sustainable development demands of research against what science can offer in response: understanding complex society-environment interrelations calls for interdisciplinary cooperation; managing “wicked problems” with incomplete knowledge and contradictory agendas calls for transdisciplinary cooperation; multi-level interactions from local to global call for multi-level, multi-stakeholder approaches; and non-linear, accelerating change calls for flexible, creative research methods, alongside teaching that builds knowledge, skills, and values together rather than knowledge alone. A worked example makes the case: research on land degradation in the Ethiopian highlands, where 80% of the population depends directly on the land, cannot be solved with biophysical methods alone, since any viable solution has to be simultaneously environmentally sound, economically viable, and socially compatible, which is only possible by integrating biophysical and socio-economic methods within one research design (Herweg et al., 2017). A parallel case from Kenya’s Ewaso Ng’iro river basin makes the same point for water: rising abstraction and seasonal drying of the river needed a combination of technical, social, and institutional solutions, plus sustained multi-level stakeholder engagement, not a purely hydrological fix.
📖 Textbook: Sustainability science: origins and understanding · Types of knowledge for sustainable development · Empirical-analytical vs normative · Global challenges as wicked problems

title: Week 2 Reader: Interlinkages of Sustainability Dimensions and Role of Science & Higher Education
text:
The role of higher education
If research needs to change, so does the institution that produces most of it. Price et al. (2021) argue that universities have an “untapped potential” for sustainability leadership precisely because a business-as-usual approach has not produced a breakthrough on global challenges: universities train the researchers, teachers, administrators, and private- and public-sector professionals who will go on to shape sustainable development in practice, in “many places” at once, which is a different kind of leverage than any single research project has on its own.
The session illustrates this with three institutional examples, not as a benchmark to copy but as a set of concrete starting points:

University of Bern: sustainability as one of five institutional priority topics, a commitment to climate neutrality by 2025, a cross-faculty Commission for Sustainable Development, a joint Sustainability Day with other Bern institutions, funding for student sustainability projects, a teaching grant for “Promoting SD in teaching,” specific SD degree programmes (Bachelor minors and a Master’s in Sustainability Transformations), and, notably, a mandatory double lesson on SD integrated into every Bachelor’s programme university-wide, a comparatively low-cost intervention designed for maximum reach.
Addis Ababa University (and other Ethiopian universities): a dedicated Centre for Sustainability, solar energy use on campus, SD integrated as a taught course, and campus greening and conservation initiatives.
University of Nairobi: dedicated research centres such as the Wangari Maathai Institute of Peace and Environmental Studies, and Master’s-level programmes (biodiversity and natural resource development; sustainable urban development and environmental planning) run as integrated programmes for students from mixed disciplinary backgrounds.







Note



Adapting this for your own institution
These three institutions are illustrations, not a fixed reference set. If you are adapting this course elsewhere, replace them with sustainability initiatives from your own university, or invite participants to name their own institution’s examples during the session, the exercise works better as a mirror than as a lecture.

title: Week 2 Reader: Interlinkages of Sustainability Dimensions and Role of Science & Higher Education
text:
Reflecting on disciplinary contributions
The session uses the parable of blindfolded people each touching a different part of an elephant, one feels a trunk and thinks “snake,” another a leg and thinks “tree,” and concludes: everyone is somehow right, everyone is somehow wrong, and nobody captures the full picture alone. Applied to a concrete case, rapid urbanisation in Addis Ababa, this maps onto real disciplinary fragments: green space, mobility, energy, agriculture, housing, industry, health, pollution, infrastructure, security, and communication are all genuinely part of the same problem, but each is usually studied, and taught, by a different discipline in isolation.
Herweg et al. (2021) offer a more systematic way to locate a given discipline’s contribution to SD, since the link is often “hidden or indirect” rather than obvious. They distinguish four possible interfaces: a discipline’s research topics may connect directly to core SD issues (resource degradation, migration, globalisation); its research methodology may help measure or track key variables regardless of topic; its theory may contribute to conceptual debates about SD; and its application may have direct real-world SD impact (a new technology, a new regulation, a piece of ESD curriculum). Mapped against the three sustainability dimensions, this produces a 4×3 grid that any discipline can use to locate its own contribution. The slides work through psychology as a worked example: research topics might include behavioural interventions for pro-environmental behaviour or community resilience; methodology might range from surveys to longitudinal studies; theory might draw on the Theory of Planned Behaviour or ecopsychology; and application might mean behaviour-change campaigns or workplace well-being programmes, none of which is “environmental psychology” in name, but all of it substantively connected to SD once the grid makes the connection explicit.
The University of Bern’s own “Links to SD” information sheets (bne.unibe.ch) apply exactly this exercise across every discipline taught at the university, specifically to help lecturers locate their own course content within SD rather than treating sustainability as an add-on subject.

title: Week 2 Reader: Interlinkages of Sustainability Dimensions and Role of Science & Higher Education
text:
Key messages

Every sustainability challenge needs to be examined from the perspective of all three (or more) dimensions at once, not one at a time.
Research for sustainable development requires inter- and transdisciplinary approaches, since no single discipline captures a “wicked problem” fully.
Higher education institutions, and their individual lecturers, carry real responsibility for equipping future leaders to advance sustainable development.
Every discipline holds knowledge that can support sustainable development, even where the connection is not immediately obvious.

title: Week 2 Reader: Interlinkages of Sustainability Dimensions and Role of Science & Higher Education
text:
Looking ahead: Task after Session 2
Building on this session, the task is to identify concrete opportunities to incorporate SD into your own course, using the SDGs (or another framework relevant to your context), global sustainability challenges, or the different worldviews introduced in Week 1, and to articulate explicitly what links your own discipline has with sustainable development. The four-interface grid (research topics, methodology, theory, application) introduced above is a direct tool for that task, not just an illustration.


← Back to Session 02

title: Week 3 Reader: Education for Sustainable Development (ESD) & Constructive Alignment
text:
This reader expands on the Week 3 slides: it walks through the same concepts in more depth, with the reasoning and sources behind each slide spelled out. Use it to prepare, to revisit after the session, or as a stand-alone introduction if you are adapting this course and did not attend the live delivery. Also available as a downloadable PDF.
Unlike Weeks 1 and 2, this session is about pedagogy and course design rather than sustainability content, so most of it does not map onto the Basics of Sustainability textbook, which is a content textbook, not a teaching-methods one. Where it genuinely does connect (the two worked examples below), the link is there; where it does not, the reader relies on its own sources instead.

title: Week 3 Reader: Education for Sustainable Development (ESD) & Constructive Alignment
section: From “spray and pray” to Education for Sustainable Development
text:
From “spray and pray” to Education for Sustainable Development
The session opens with a deliberately unflattering image: “spray and pray”, the assumption that if students are exposed to enough scientific facts, they will somehow go on to change the world professionally once they leave the classroom. Naming this as the default and then setting it aside is the point of the session: sustainability challenges are complex enough that information alone rarely changes what people do with it, which is why the UN’s 2030 Agenda explicitly calls for a new kind of science and a new kind of education, not just more of the same content delivered more urgently.
UNESCO defines Education for Sustainable Development (ESD) as an approach that “gives learners of all ages the knowledge, skills, values and agency to address interconnected global challenges including climate change, loss of biodiversity, unsustainable use of resources, and inequality,” empowering them “to make informed decisions and take individual and collective action to change society and care for the planet.” UNESCO’s 2021 Berlin Declaration goes further, calling ESD “the foundation for the required transformation,” equipping people to become change agents rather than informed bystanders. The founding value behind both formulations is respect: for other people, for future generations, and for the planet and what it provides.
A useful distinction sharpens what this actually means in practice: education about sustainable development is an awareness lesson or theoretical discussion, information transfer. Education for sustainable development uses education as a tool to build the capacity to act, giving people knowledge and skills for lifelong learning so they can find new solutions to environmental, economic, and social problems themselves. The “about” version can leave a course entirely unchanged in structure while adding sustainability as a topic; the “for” version changes what students are asked to do, not just what they are told.
ESD is not a peripheral add-on to the SDGs, it is written into them directly. SDG 4 (Quality Education) is a stand-alone goal, but its Target 4.7 specifically commits UN member states to ensuring that, by 2030, all learners acquire the knowledge and skills to promote sustainable development, explicitly including education for sustainable development, human rights, gender equality, and global citizenship. The African Union’s Agenda 2063 makes a parallel commitment under Goal 2, “Well Educated Citizens and Skills Revolution,” underpinned by science, technology, and innovation.

title: Week 3 Reader: Education for Sustainable Development (ESD) & Constructive Alignment
text:
Competences, not just content
ESD is built around competences rather than content coverage. Following Abelha et al. (2020), a competence is an umbrella term for a person’s knowledge, skills, and abilities: it presumes a background of prior resources (knowledge, skills, experience, values), requires those resources to be mobilised in a specific context (such as solving a real problem), and is only visible once applied in that context. This is a stronger claim than it might first sound: a competence is not “knowing about” something, it is being able to do something with what you know, in a situation where it actually matters.
This competence orientation is not abstract policy language, it is already reshaping curricula on the ground. Kenya’s shift from the older 8-4-4 system (an objective-driven, content-based curriculum with performance-based assessment) to the competence-based 2-6-3-3-3 system is one concrete example: the newer system foregrounds student-centred teaching and practical experience, aiming to build 21st-century skills such as critical thinking and problem-solving, with creativity, inclusivity, and sustainable development named as core competences expected of every learner.
Rieckmann (2018) identifies three pedagogical shifts that follow from taking competences seriously: knowledge should be actively constructed by learners rather than transferred to them (the educator becomes a facilitator of learning processes, not a source of facts); learners should engage in action and reflect on their own experience of it (the educator’s job is to create environments that prompt that reflection); and learners should be empowered to question and change how they see and think about the world (the educator becomes someone who challenges learners, not just informs them). Translated into concrete teaching principles: work on real-world problems and be solution-oriented, bring students from different disciplines together rather than teaching within a single subject silo, build on participation and cooperation, involve practitioners, foreground values-based learning and critical thinking over memorisation, and favour locally relevant information over generic national or global material.

title: Week 3 Reader: Education for Sustainable Development (ESD) & Constructive Alignment
text:
Constructive alignment
Constructive alignment, introduced by John Biggs in the mid-1990s, is the design tool this session uses to translate ESD principles into an actual course unit. The idea is that three elements have to be deliberately aligned with each other: learning outcomes (what competences the course is meant to build), learning activities (the teaching-learning arrangements that give students a chance to build them), and assessment (how you find out whether they actually did). The word “constructive” signals that learners make content meaningful themselves, through the learning activities, rather than having meaning delivered to them ready-made.
In practice, this means answering three questions in sequence and keeping the answers consistent with each other: What should students know or be able to do by the end (learning outcomes)? What activities will actually help them get there (learning activities)? And how will you know if they got there (assessment)? A course can have excellent learning outcomes and a rigorous exam and still fail at constructive alignment, if the learning activities in between do not actually build toward what the outcomes promise and the assessment then tests.
Learning outcomes should be formulated in an action-oriented way, specifying not just what learners should know but what they should be able to do with it, including being able to self-assess their own attitudes and values by the end of the course. A standard tool for writing them precisely is a taxonomy of active verbs pegged to performance level: remembering uses verbs like recall, name, list, or cite; understanding uses explain, describe, compare, or interpret; problem-solving uses apply, analyse, design, justify, or create. Choosing the verb is not a wording exercise, it commits you to a specific, checkable level of performance.
Learning activities that foster sustainability competences tend to share a family resemblance: dialogic strategies (discussion, debate, dialogue), critical reflection on locally and globally relevant issues, hypothetical or real cases (role-play, simulation, case studies), collaboration on shared projects, experiential activities such as community action, interdisciplinary joint problem-framing, project- or problem-based learning, and action-research cycles of planning, acting, observing, and reflecting (Tejedor et al., 2019).
Assessment has to be valid, meaning it actually tests what the course intended to teach, and it comes in several recognisable formats: solving set tasks, explaining or defining terms in one’s own words, working through real or constructed cases, writing essays or technical reports, or writing reviews and critical statements. Assessment also serves two distinct functions that are easy to conflate: a formative function during the course, giving learners feedback on where they currently stand so they can adjust; and a summative function at the end, where the result “counts” toward a grade or certificate. A course that only assesses summatively gives students no chance to course-correct before the result is final.

title: Week 3 Reader: Education for Sustainable Development (ESD) & Constructive Alignment
text:
Two worked examples
The session works through two full constructive-alignment examples end to end, each mapped across the three sustainability dimensions (environment, society, economy) before the learning outcomes, activities, and assessment are built on top.
Example 1: Land degradation. The topics span all three dimensions: environmentally, depletion of natural resources (soil fertility, water quality, biodiversity), soil erosion, and rising temperatures; socially, effects on land tenure systems, migration patterns, and access to resources, which can generate conflict within communities; economically, reduced agricultural productivity and income, migration pressure, and shifting power dynamics around trade and resource extraction. The resulting learning outcomes are deliberately spread across knowledge, skills, and attitude: understanding the causes and consequences of land degradation (knowledge), applying field observation and analysis skills during a guided site visit (skills), and demonstrating an appreciation for the perspectives of stakeholders affected by land degradation gathered through exchanges and interviews (attitude). The learning activities, a presentation, a guided field visit, and stakeholder interviews, and the assessment, a written report covering environmental, societal, and economic aspects, are built to match.
Example 2: Urban migration. Structured the same way: environmentally, urban expansion, habitat loss, deforestation, and rising resource consumption; socially, strain on urban infrastructure and services, and increased inequality; economically, globalisation of labour markets and unequal distribution of resources and opportunities. Learning outcomes again span knowledge (understanding the drivers of urban migration), skills (collecting and presenting information through multiple media, such as video and photography), and attitude (engaging constructively in group debate and proposing solutions). Learning activities include brainstorming, multimedia information-gathering, and structured debate; assessment is a written reflection proposing a solution and a strategy, alongside a short report built partly from interviews with community elders.






Note



Adapting the worked examples
Both examples were built for the Ethiopia/Kenya pilot cohorts and use topics with direct local relevance there. If you are adapting this course for a different context, keep the three-dimension table structure and the knowledge/skills/attitude split, they are the transferable part, but swap in a topic your own participants will recognise from their own discipline and region.


📖 Textbook: Land use change covers the land degradation example’s environmental dimension in more depth (soil degradation, land tenure and land rights, land use conflicts). The urban migration example does not have a direct match in the textbook, which does not currently treat urbanisation or migration as a dedicated topic.

title: Week 3 Reader: Education for Sustainable Development (ESD) & Constructive Alignment
text:
Reflection: the muddiest point
The session closes with a “muddiest point” reflection: participants write down the most difficult or confusing part of the session, which the facilitator then reviews and addresses at the start of the next session, rather than leaving it unresolved. It is a small technique, but it does something a general “any questions?” rarely achieves: it surfaces confusion that participants might not feel confident raising out loud, and it commits the facilitator to actually closing the loop.

title: Week 3 Reader: Education for Sustainable Development (ESD) & Constructive Alignment
section: Looking ahead: your own Action Plan
text:
Looking ahead: your own Action Plan
The task after this session is to put constructive alignment into practice: find a topic related to sustainable development in your own discipline, and design a session for it, formulating at least three learning outcomes, choosing learning activities that actively engage students with SD and ESD principles, and designing a matching assessment format. This is the piece of the overall ESD Action Plan you will present in Session 4, so it is worth treating as a real design exercise, not a hypothetical one, ideally for a session you could actually teach.


← Back to Session 03

title: Week 4 Reader: Presentation of Action Plans
text: Session 4 does not introduce new sustainability content. It is where the three previous sessions come together in your own ESD Action Plan. This reader is shorter than the others on purpose: it is a guide to finishing a strong Action Plan and presenting it well, not a new set of concepts to learn. Also available as a downloadable PDF.

title: Week 4 Reader: Presentation of Action Plans
section: What the Action Plan is actually made of
text:
What the Action Plan is actually made of
By this session, your Action Plan already has three parts, one from each of the previous sessions, and this session asks you to bring them together into a single short presentation:

From Session 1: a review of how sustainable development currently shows up (or doesn’t) in your own teaching content and syllabi, using the dimensions, frameworks, and historical grounding covered there as your reference points.
From Session 2: the concrete opportunities you identified to bring SD into your course, framed through the SDGs, Agenda 2063, or another relevant framework, and articulated through your own discipline’s specific links to sustainability.
From Session 3: a fully developed lesson or session built with constructive alignment, at least three learning outcomes, learning activities that actively engage students with those outcomes, and an assessment format that actually measures them.

If you want a refresher on any of these before presenting, the Week 1, Week 2, and Week 3 readers cover them in depth, including the textbook links for Sessions 1 and 2.

title: Week 4 Reader: Presentation of Action Plans
text:
Presenting in six minutes
The presentation itself is short by design, roughly six minutes per participant or group, so it works best as a structured walk-through rather than a comprehensive account. The slides suggest covering, in order: your current state (what you found in the Session 1 review), the opportunities and gaps you identified (Session 2), and the developed lesson itself (Session 3), naming its three learning outcomes, the learning activities that support them, and how you would assess them. Resist the pull to spend most of the six minutes on background and context, the constructive-alignment design is the part your listeners are there to react to and give feedback on.

title: Week 4 Reader: Presentation of Action Plans
text:
Giving useful peer feedback
Listeners are asked to take notes and prepare constructive feedback while others present. Because action plans span many different disciplines, the most useful feedback usually isn’t “does this work well within its own field,” but rather whether and how a presented idea could translate into a different field. A constructive-alignment design built for a hydrology course and one built for a literature course rarely transfer directly, but the underlying moves (a clearer learning outcome, a more active learning activity, a better-aligned assessment) usually do. Framing feedback this way is also what turns individual presentations into the basis for the collaboration discussion that follows.

title: Week 4 Reader: Presentation of Action Plans
text:
From presentations to collaboration
After the presentations, the session moves to a synthesis of the key insights that came up (recurring challenges, and where people said they need more support), followed by a structured discussion of collaboration opportunities: with other lecturers, other departments, or organisations outside academia already working on sustainability initiatives. This is where the cross-disciplinary variety of the Action Plans becomes an asset rather than a complication, the differences between disciplines are exactly what make collaboration worth pursuing, rather than everyone independently reinventing similar material.

title: Week 4 Reader: Presentation of Action Plans
text:
Closing the course
The course closes with an open reflection on the main learnings from across all four sessions, followed by a course evaluation. Since this pilot course has been delivered in different formats (fully live, self-paced online, and hybrid, across the Kenyan and Ethiopian cohorts), the evaluation should be read and adapted with that specific delivery context in mind, what worked in a live, in-person setting will not always transfer directly to a self-paced asynchronous one, and vice versa.
